r: The migration passed every staging run against a 40 GB snapshot of synthetic rows, yet died forty minutes into production. The real orders table held 1.2 billion rows and a decade of drift. The ALTER TABLE added a NOT NULL column with a default, which on PostgreSQL 10 forces a rewrite of the entire heap. That rewrite queued behind long-running checkout transactions, then requested an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that every later write had to wait out. Connection pool exhaustion alerts paged on-call within ninety seconds as requests piled up. Engineers assumed the default was metadata-only, but that fast path arrived in PostgreSQL 11, not 10. The rollback runbook, never rehearsed, cost another twenty minutes. Staging had lied by omission. Teams now shadow-migrate against full-size clones, set lock_timeout to 5 seconds, and backfill in batches before tightening constraints. Some call this discipline "expand, then squeeze."
